t: 3219. Minimum Cost for Cutting Cake II
o: Cut an m x n cake into unit pieces. Each cut along a line costs that line's fixed cost, but the same line may need to be applied to multiple current pieces, multiplying its effective price by how many perpendicular strips exist when it is cut. Cutting expensive lines early, while the piece count in the other dimension is still small, minimizes total cost. In example 1, cutting the costly vertical line (5) first costs 5 once, whereas delaying it would cost 5 three times.
k: A horizontal cut performed when there are v vertical strips costs horizontalCut[i] * v.
Greedy: always perform the remaining cut with the largest cost next — an exchange argument shows swapping any two consecutive cuts never helps.
Sort both arrays descending and merge, multiplying by the current strip count of the perpendicular direction.

a.i: Sort all cuts by cost descending. Process cuts in that order: a horizontal cut multiplies its cost by the current number of vertical pieces, and vice versa. An exchange argument proves optimality: if a cheaper cut is done before a pricier one, swapping them changes total cost by (cheap·a + pricey·b) vs (pricey·a + cheap·b) where a <= b, and doing the pricey one first is never worse.
s: Sort horizontalCut and verticalCut in descending order.
Maintain hp = 1 horizontal pieces and vp = 1 vertical pieces.
Repeatedly take the larger remaining cut: add cost * (perpendicular piece count) and increment that direction's piece count.
a.t: O((m + n) log(m + n)) — sorting dominates; the merge is linear
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond sorting (or O(m + n) if inputs must not be mutated)

a.i: Push every cut (cost, orientation) into a max-heap and repeatedly pop the most expensive remaining cut, applying the same multiplication rule. This is equivalent to sorting but expresses the 'always take the largest' policy directly and handles streamed cut costs naturally.
s: Insert all horizontal cuts tagged H and vertical cuts tagged V into a max-heap keyed by cost.
Pop cuts one at a time, adding cost times the current perpendicular piece count and updating counts.
a.t: O((m + n) log(m + n)) — heap operations dominate

w: Use 64-bit accumulation: costs up to 1000 multiplied by up to 1e5 pieces overflow 32 bits. Ties between equal-cost cuts can be broken arbitrarily. Common pitfalls: multiplying by the wrong direction's count, or forgetting that each line is cut once per current strip. Follow-up: if costs depended on piece size, the greedy breaks and one would need a different strategy.
